# Anchor here() to the course folder, regardless of where the R session started
here::i_am("chapters/ch07-catcher-framing/lecture/L19-21-catcher-framing.qmd")
here() starts at /Users/philip/Library/CloudStorage/OneDrive-USAFA(AFAcademy.AF.edu)/usafa-or476-fall26
data_dir <- here::here("data")
taken_path <- file.path(data_dir, "sc_taken_2022.rds")

# Download and build the season only if the taken-pitch file does not exist yet
if (!file.exists(taken_path)) {
  day_dir <- file.path(data_dir, "savant_2022")
  dir.create(day_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

  # One request per day; each day is cached so an interrupted run resumes
  savant_day <- function(date) {
    path <- file.path(day_dir, paste0(date, ".rds"))
    if (!file.exists(path)) {
      url <- paste0(
        "https://baseballsavant.mlb.com/statcast_search/csv?all=true&hfGT=R%7C",
        "&game_date_gt=", date, "&game_date_lt=", date, "&type=details"
      )
      write_rds(read_csv(url, col_types = cols(.default = col_character())), path)
    }
    read_rds(path)
  }

  sc2022 <- seq(as.Date("2022-04-07"), as.Date("2022-10-05"), by = "day") |>
    as.character() |>
    map(savant_day, .progress = TRUE) |>
    list_rbind() |>
    type_convert()
  write_rds(sc2022, file.path(data_dir, "statcast_2022.rds"))

  sc_taken <- sc2022 |>
    mutate(
      Outcome = case_when(
        description %in% c("ball", "blocked_ball", "pitchout",
                           "hit_by_pitch") ~ "ball",
        description == "called_strike" ~ "called_strike",
        .default = "swing"
      ),
      Home = ifelse(inning_topbot == "Bot", 1, 0),
      Count = paste(balls, strikes, sep = "-")
    ) |>
    filter(Outcome != "swing") |>
    select(pitch_type, release_speed, description, stand, p_throws, Outcome,
           plate_x, plate_z, fielder_2_1 = fielder_2, pitcher, batter,
           Count, Home, zone)
  write_rds(sc_taken, taken_path, compress = "xz")
}

sc_taken <- read_rds(taken_path)

Fit a predicted called strike model based on pitch location

library(mgcv)

strike_mod <- gam(
  Outcome == "called_strike" ~ s(plate_x, plate_z), 
  family = binomial, 
  data = taken
)

How does the GAM compare to other models? Each model below was trained on 10,000, 50,000, and 300,000 pitches from 2022 and evaluated on the same 50,000 held-out pitches.

Add the predicted probability of a strike to each taken pitch. The rows of hats are in the same order as taken.

taken <- taken |>
  mutate(prob_strike = hats$.fitted)

How would we use these data to measure the framing ability of each catcher?

Look up player names from MLBAM IDs. The Chadwick register is downloaded once and saved to data/.

id_path <- file.path(data_dir, "player_ids.rds")
if (!file.exists(id_path)) {
  baseballr::chadwick_player_lu() |>
    filter(!is.na(key_mlbam)) |>
    transmute(mlb_id = key_mlbam, name = paste(name_first, name_last)) |>
    write_rds(id_path)
}
player_names <- read_rds(id_path)

Compare each catcher’s called strikes to the strikes the GAM expected. A positive strikes_added means the catcher received more strikes than the pitch locations predict.

framing_table <- function(pitches) {
  pitches |>
    group_by(fielder_2_1) |>
    summarize(
      pitches = n(),
      called_strikes = sum(Outcome == "called_strike"),
      expected_strikes = sum(prob_strike),
      strikes_added = called_strikes - expected_strikes
    ) |>
    left_join(player_names, by = c("fielder_2_1" = "mlb_id")) |>
    relocate(catcher = name) |>
    slice_max(strikes_added, n = 20)
}

Should every taken pitch count toward a catcher’s framing?

Keep only borderline pitches, those within buffer feet of the edge of the rulebook zone.

x_edge <- (plate_width/2)/12
z_bot <- 1.5
z_top <- 3.6
buffer <- 0.25  # feet, about 3 inches

borderline <- taken |>
  filter(
    abs(plate_x) <= x_edge + buffer,
    between(plate_z, z_bot - buffer, z_top + buffer),
    !(abs(plate_x) <= x_edge - buffer &
        between(plate_z, z_bot + buffer, z_top - buffer))
  )

  aes(color = Outcome) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.2) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = -x_edge - buffer, xmax = x_edge + buffer,
           ymin = z_bot - buffer, ymax = z_top + buffer,
           fill = NA, color = "gray40", linetype = "dashed") +
  annotate("rect", xmin = -x_edge + buffer, xmax = x_edge - buffer,
           ymin = z_bot + buffer, ymax = z_top - buffer,

How many runs is one extra strike worth? Turning a ball into a strike changes run expectancy, and the size of that change depends on the count. We use Statcast’s delta_run_exp, the change in run expectancy on each pitch.

sc2022 <- read_rds(file.path(data_dir, "statcast_2022.rds"))

count_values <- sc2022 |>
  filter(description %in% c("ball", "called_strike")) |>
  group_by(balls, strikes, description) |>
  summarize(run_value = mean(delta_run_exp, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = description, values_from = run_value) |>
  mutate(
    Count = paste(balls, strikes, sep = "-"),
    strike_value = ball - called_strike
  )

For scale, compare to the top hitters. Recall from Chapter 5 that the linear weight of an event is the average change in run expectancy over the plate appearances that end in that event.

  group_by(game_pk, at_bat_number) |>
  summarize(
    batter = first(batter),

    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(event), event != "truncated_pa")

Before we trust this ranking, we must address two problems.

Part A: Why Do We Need a New Model?

Problem 1: several players influence every call. The catcher, pitcher, batter, and umpire all contribute to each called strike. However, strikes_added gives all of the credit to the catcher. Thus, a catcher who receives pitches from a staff with excellent command may look like a better framer than the catcher truly is.

Problem 2: catchers do not catch the same number of pitches. Some catchers receive thousands of pitches in a season, while others receive fewer than 10. A rate based on 10 pitches is mostly “luck,” so it is difficult to identify the best framer with a rate statistic.

With this framework in mind, we need a method that (1) estimates the catcher, pitcher, and batter effects at the same time, and (2) trusts a small sample less than a large one. A mixed-effects model does both.

Part B: A Primer on Mixed-Effects Models

In this section, we focus on why and when we use mixed-effects models rather than on how they are estimated.

Three Ways to Handle Groups

Our pitches are grouped by catcher. In general, there are three ways to estimate an effect for each group.

Approach Assumption Sample model Problem
Complete pooling Every catcher is identical. called_strike ~ prob_strike Cannot measure framing at all.
No pooling Every catcher is unrelated to every other catcher. called_strike ~ prob_strike + catcher Small samples produce extreme estimates.
Partial pooling Catchers differ, but they come from a common population. called_strike ~ prob_strike + (1 | catcher) We must also estimate how much catchers differ.
  • Complete pooling uses only the league. No pooling uses only the catcher.
  • Partial pooling is a compromise between the two.
  • In the no-pooling model, catcher is a factor, so each catcher receives a separate coefficient. The (1 | catcher) term is new, and we explain it below.

Why Partial Pooling Works

The partial-pooling estimate for catcher \(j\) is approximately a weighted average of the catcher’s own rate and the league average:

\[ \text{estimate}_j \approx w_j \times (\text{catcher } j\text{'s own rate}) + (1 - w_j) \times (\text{league average}), \qquad w_j = \frac{n_j}{n_j + k}, \qquad k = \frac{\sigma^2_{\text{luck}}}{\sigma^2_{\text{skill}}}, \]

where

  • \(n_j\) is the number of pitches caught by catcher \(j\),
  • \(\sigma^2_{\text{luck}} = \bar{p}(1 - \bar{p})\) is the variance of a single pitch (strike or ball) when the league strike rate is \(\bar{p}\), and
  • \(\sigma^2_{\text{skill}}\) is the variance of true framing skill across catchers.

Notice that

  • a large \(n_j\) gives \(w_j \approx 1\), so we trust the catcher’s own rate;
  • a small \(n_j\) gives \(w_j \approx 0\), so we “shrink” the estimate toward the league average; and
  • \(w_j\) is the reliability of catcher \(j\)’s rate from L05. In Chapter 8, we will see the same idea as “regression to the mean.”

We set the values that we will use in the simulation below.

league_rate <- 0.35  # average called strike rate on borderline pitches
skill_sd <- 0.03     # standard deviation of true framing skill (3 percentage points)
k <- (league_rate * (1 - league_rate)) / skill_sd^2
k
[1] 252.7778
  • The numerator, league_rate * (1 - league_rate), is \(\sigma^2_{\text{luck}}\), the variance of one pitch that is a strike with probability 0.35.
  • The denominator, skill_sd^2, is \(\sigma^2_{\text{skill}}\).
  • Thus, \(k \approx 253\). Intuitively, a catcher needs about 253 pitches before their own rate receives half of the weight.

A Simulation Where We Know the Truth

  • In real data, we never observe a catcher’s true skill.
  • In a simulation, we do. We create 40 catchers with known skill and between 20 and 3,000 pitches each.
set.seed(476)
n_catchers <- 40
sim <- tibble(
  catcher = paste0("C", 1:n_catchers),
  pitches = round(exp(runif(n_catchers, log(20), log(3000)))),
  true_skill = rnorm(n_catchers, mean = 0, sd = skill_sd)
) |>
  mutate(strikes = rbinom(n_catchers, pitches, league_rate + true_skill))
sim

We estimate each catcher’s skill three ways:

  • Complete pooling: every catcher has a skill of 0.
  • No pooling: each catcher’s own strike rate minus the league rate.
  • Partial pooling: a mixed-effects model fit with glmer() from the lme4 package.
library(lme4)
Loading required package: Matrix

Attaching package: 'Matrix'

sim_mod <- glmer(
  cbind(strikes, pitches - strikes) ~ 1 + (1 | catcher),
  family = binomial,
  data = sim
)

sim <- sim |>
  mutate(
    complete_pooling = 0,
    no_pooling = strikes / pitches - league_rate,
    partial_pooling = predict(sim_mod, type = "response") - league_rate
  )

Estimated versus true skill. The dashed line is a perfect estimate.

sim_long <- sim |>
  pivot_longer(c(complete_pooling, no_pooling, partial_pooling),
               names_to = "approach", values_to = "estimate") |>
  mutate(approach = factor(
    approach,
    levels = c("complete_pooling", "no_pooling", "partial_pooling"),
    labels = c("Complete pooling", "No pooling", "Partial pooling")
  ))

  geom_abline(linetype = "dashed", color = "gray50") +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  facet_wrap(~ approach) +
  scale_color_viridis_c(trans = "log10", direction = -1) +
  labs(x = "True framing skill (extra strike probability)",
       y = "Estimated framing skill", color = "Pitches")
  • Complete pooling ignores every real difference.
  • No pooling scatters the small samples (yellow) far from the line.
  • Partial pooling pulls the small samples toward 0 and leaves the large samples on the line.

  group_by(approach) |>
  summarize(rmse = sqrt(mean((estimate - true_skill)^2)))

Each arrow runs from the no-pooling estimate to the partial-pooling estimate.

shrinkage_plot <- function(data, y_label) {
  ggplot(data, aes(x = pitches)) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "gray50") +
    geom_segment(aes(xend = pitches, y = no_pooling, yend = partial_pooling),
                 arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.08, "inches")), color = "gray60") +
    geom_point(aes(y = no_pooling, color = "No pooling")) +
    geom_point(aes(y = partial_pooling, color = "Partial pooling")) +
    scale_color_manual(values = c("No pooling" = crc_fc[2],
                                  "Partial pooling" = crc_fc[1])) +
    scale_x_log10() +
    labs(x = "Pitches caught (log scale)", y = y_label, color = NULL)
}

shrinkage_plot(sim, "Estimated framing skill")
  • Small samples (left) move the most. Large samples (right) barely move.
  • This is the “I don’t believe you yet” behavior of partial pooling.

When Should We Use a Mixed-Effects Model?

Every grouping in a model is either a fixed effect or a random effect.

Use a random effect when… Use a fixed effect when…
there are many groups (120 catchers). there are only a few groups (home and away).
we view the groups as a sample from a larger population (this year’s catchers). the groups are the complete set of possibilities (the 12 ball-strike counts).
some groups are small (a catcher with 8 pitches). every group has plenty of data (thousands of pitches per count).
we care about the population of groups and want to shrink small samples. we want to compare those exact groups directly (left-handed versus right-handed batters).
  • Mixed-effects models are especially useful when several groupings cross one another. Every pitch has a catcher, a pitcher, and a batter.
  • A single model can contain both. Model A uses a fixed effect for prob_strike and a random effect for the catcher.

Class activity. Each pair below contains one fixed effect and one random effect. Which is which, and why?

  1. In a model of called strikes: (a) the ball-strike count, or (b) the home plate umpire.
  2. In a model of called strikes: (a) pitch type (four-seam, slider, changeup, and so on), or (b) the individual pitcher.
  3. In a model of maintenance failures: (a) aircraft type (C-17, KC-135, F-16), or (b) the individual aircraft (tail number).
  4. In a model of cadet GPA: (a) class year (four classes), or (b) cadet squadron.
NoteDiscussion
  1. Count is fixed. There are only 12 counts, they are every count that exists, and each has thousands of pitches. Umpire is random. There are roughly 90 umpires, and some work far fewer games than others.
  2. Pitch type is fixed. There are a handful of types, each has thousands of pitches, and we want to compare specific types. Pitcher is random. There are 870 pitchers, and many threw only a few innings.
  3. Aircraft type is fixed. There are a few types, and we care about each one. Tail number is random. There are many aircraft, and some have flown far fewer hours than others.
  4. Class year is fixed. There are exactly four classes, each with about 1,000 cadets. Squadron is random. There are 40 squadrons, and we view them as a sample of the squadrons that could exist.

Reading the Model Syntax

glmer() uses the same formula syntax as glm(), plus one new term.

Term Meaning
Outcome == "called_strike" The response: was the taken pitch called a strike?
prob_strike A fixed effect: the GAM probability of a strike from the pitch location.
(1 | fielder_2_1) A random effect: each catcher has an intercept, drawn from a normal distribution with mean 0 and standard deviation \(s_c\).
family = binomial The response is a strike or a ball. We explain this with Model A below.

Three functions read the fitted model:

  • fixef(): the fixed effects.
  • VarCorr(): \(s_c\), how much catchers truly differ.
  • ranef(): the partial-pooling estimate for each catcher.

Part C: Modeling Catcher Framing (Section 7.5)

In this section, we fit the two models from Section 7.5 to every taken pitch of 2022, rather than to the textbook’s sample of 50,000 pitches.

Model A: Catcher Effects Only

\[ \log\frac{p_j}{1-p_j} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot \texttt{prob\_strike}_j + \alpha_{c(j)}, \]

  • \(p_j\) is the probability that pitch \(j\) is called a strike.
  • The right side adds three pieces: a baseline \(\beta_0\), the location effect \(\beta_1 \cdot \texttt{prob\_strike}_j\), and the effect \(\alpha_{c(j)}\) of the catcher who received pitch \(j\).

Notice that the code below uses Outcome == "called_strike" as the response, but the equation has \(\log\frac{p_j}{1-p_j}\) on the left. The two match as follows:

Code Equation
Outcome == "called_strike" The outcome we observe: a strike (TRUE) or a ball (FALSE). We model its probability, \(p_j\).
family = binomial The outcome is a strike or a ball, so the right side predicts the log-odds, \(\log\frac{p_j}{1-p_j}\).
prob_strike \(\beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot \texttt{prob\_strike}_j\)
(1 | fielder_2_1) \(\alpha_{c(j)}\)
  • Why the log-odds? The right side can be any number, but a probability must stay between 0 and 1. The log-odds can also be any number, so every value on the right side corresponds to a valid probability.
  • We used the same setup for the GAM, which also had family = binomial. The function plogis() converts the log-odds back to a probability.
mod_a <- glmer(
  Outcome == "called_strike" ~ prob_strike + (1 | fielder_2_1),
  family = binomial,
  data = taken
)
fixef(mod_a)
(Intercept) prob_strike 
  -4.003539    7.627854 
VarCorr(mod_a)
 Groups      Name        Std.Dev.
 fielder_2_1 (Intercept) 0.2117
  • The catcher effects are on the log-odds scale.
  • We convert them to strikes. For each pitch, we compute the log-odds with and without the catcher’s effect, convert both to probabilities with plogis(), and take the difference. Summing over the season gives strikes added.
catcher_strikes <- function(mod) {
  eta <- predict(mod, type = "link")
  b <- ranef(mod)$fielder_2_1[as.character(taken$fielder_2_1), 1]
  taken |>
    mutate(strikes = plogis(eta) - plogis(eta - b)) |>
    group_by(fielder_2_1) |>
    summarize(strikes_added = sum(strikes))
}

Complete, No, and Partial Pooling with Real Data

Please note that our naive strikes_added is the no-pooling estimate.

pooling <- taken |>
  group_by(fielder_2_1) |>
  summarize(
    pitches = n(),
    no_pooling = sum(Outcome == "called_strike") - sum(prob_strike)
  ) |>
  left_join(
    catcher_strikes(mod_a) |> rename(partial_pooling = strikes_added),
    by = "fielder_2_1"
  ) |>
  mutate(complete_pooling = 0) |>
  left_join(player_names, by = c("fielder_2_1" = "mlb_id")) |>
  relocate(catcher = name)

  • Mercedes (11 pitches) and Sands (8 pitches): the highest and lowest rates in baseball with no pooling, and nearly 0 with partial pooling. The textbook’s 50,000-pitch sample ranks Sands as the best framer.

Model B: Adding Pitcher and Batter Effects

\[ \log\frac{p_j}{1-p_j} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot \texttt{prob\_strike}_j + \alpha_{c(j)} + \gamma_{p(j)} + \delta_{b(j)}, \]

where \(\gamma_{p(j)}\) is the effect of the pitcher and \(\delta_{b(j)}\) is the effect of the batter. This model takes about 1 to 2 minutes to fit.

mod_b <- glmer(
  Outcome == "called_strike" ~ prob_strike +
    (1 | fielder_2_1) + (1 | batter) + (1 | pitcher),
  family = binomial,
  data = taken
)
VarCorr(mod_b)
 Groups      Name        Std.Dev.
 pitcher     (Intercept) 0.22764 
 batter      (Intercept) 0.19242 
 fielder_2_1 (Intercept) 0.20481
  • Standard deviations: pitcher 0.23, catcher 0.20, batter 0.19.
  • The pitcher is the largest source of variation. The catcher is about as important as the batter.

Naive, Model A, and Model B strikes added for the top 15 catchers, with Model B converted to runs.

framing_compare <- pooling |>
  select(catcher, fielder_2_1, pitches, naive = no_pooling, model_a = partial_pooling) |>
  left_join(
    catcher_strikes(mod_b) |> rename(model_b = strikes_added),
    by = "fielder_2_1"
  ) |>
  mutate(runs_b = model_b * strike_value) |>
  arrange(desc(model_b))

Revisiting the Two Problems

  1. Several players influence every call. Solved in part. Model B estimates the catcher, pitcher, and batter effects at the same time.
  2. Unequal sample sizes. Solved. Partial pooling shrinks small samples toward the league average.

What the model still leaves out:

  • Umpires. The umpire column is empty. With umpire data from another source, we would add (1 | umpire).
  • Count. Recall from Chapter 6 that the zone changes with the count. We could add Count as a fixed effect.
  • Batter height. The GAM uses one zone for every batter.

Thus, the mixed-effects model is not a complete analysis of framing, but it addresses both problems from Part A, and the same approach applies to any problem in which we must separate the contributions of several players.
